summary: Same idea and same color/fade physics — random pixels ignite at a full-saturation random hue and decay exponentially to black — but at the port's untouched default the ignition rate is ~12x the original's and the fade is too fast to be visible, so the strip reads as per-frame confetti instead of the original's gentle twinkle-and-fade.
observations: Structure/color match exactly: on both sides individual pixels ignite at a random, fully-saturated hue (mean saturation 1.000 on both, measured over 60 s of ignition events) and then decay smoothly toward black with no spatial motion — nothing travels along the strip on either side.

Hue distribution is uniform and identical: over a 60 s sample of ignition events, 12 x 30-degree hue bins hold orig 8,10,13,9,6,10,9,10,9,11,6,10 (n=111) and port 20,22,17,16,16,12,19,16,21,21,15,20 (n=215) — flat on both, no palette restriction or drift on either side.

Both sides are single-regime: a 60 s / 5 fps survey shows the same texture end to end on each, no mode rotation, no long-period cycle, no drift (both brightnessTrend steady, meanBrightness ~21-23 orig across all windows). A --skip 30 late window is identical to t=0.

Both sides are time-based, not frame-stepped: the original's per-frame decay ratio is 0.90 at 20 fps and 0.955 at 40 fps (0.955^2 = 0.912), and the port's is 0.885 at 20 fps and 0.944 at 40 fps — no frame-rate coupling mismatch.

MAIN DIVERGENCE (rate). Counting ignitions (pixel brightness rising frame-to-frame) over 40 consecutive frames on the default 60 px strip at 20 fps: original 2.41 ignitions/frame; port at its untouched default 29.41 ignitions/frame — ~12x. Motion stat: orig avg 4, port avg 49 (baseline, 6 s / 20 fps); same at seed 7 (4 vs 49).

The waterfalls show this directly: the original's orig.png is made of tall vertical streaks (each ignition persists ~15-30 frames as it fades), while the untouched port.png is one-pixel-tall speckle with no vertical continuity at all. A --dump of 8 consecutive frames confirms it: the original's pixel 6 runs 65,0,70 -> 59,0,63 -> 53,0,57 -> 47,0,51 (same hue, ~0.90/frame decay), whereas every port pixel is a completely different color on every frame.

The port's Speed dial does not reach the original anywhere in its range. At sliderSpeed=0 (bottom of range) the port becomes visually very close to the original — streaky waterfall, motion 8 vs orig 4, meanBrightness 23 vs 21 — but still runs ~2x fast: 4.90 ignitions/frame vs 2.41, and 215 vs 111 ignition events over the same 60 s sample.

Fade half-life at the port's slowest setting is also slightly short: orig ~0.90/frame at 20 fps = ~0.33 s half-life; port at sliderSpeed=0 ~0.885/frame = ~0.28 s (~15% faster). Peak-brightness distribution matches well (orig median peak 85 / max 235; port@0 median 77 / max 252) as does lit fraction (orig 0.673, port@0 0.660).

CONTROL-SURFACE MISMATCH: the original exposes NO controls at all (empty control list on every run); the port adds a slider named sliderSpeed (label "Speed"). Because the original has no dial, no same-value-on-both-sides comparison is possible, and the original's behaviour corresponds to the extreme bottom of the port's dial rather than to its default.
The port's untouched default is equivalent to sliderSpeed=0.5 (probe delta 0.00 at 0.5, 35.41 at 0, 44.33 at 1), so the ~12x-too-fast state is what a user sees on load.
Behaviour is seed-independent: at --seed 7 the same numbers hold (orig motion 4, port default motion 49, port@0 motion 8).

dials.name: sliderSpeed
dials.origEffect: n/a — the original exposes no controls, so there is no corresponding dial to compare against
dials.portEffect: live and value-dependent (probe maxDelta 44.33; 0 and 1 differ from each other and from the 0.5 default). 0 = sparse twinkle with a clearly visible ~0.28 s fade tail, 4.90 ignitions/frame, meanBrightness 23, motion 8. 0.5 (default) = per-frame confetti, 29.4 ignitions/frame, motion 49. 1 = denser and brighter still (meanBrightness 42, motion 46), fade entirely invisible. Response is not monotonic in brightness between 0.5 and 1 but is monotonic in density.

feedback: Slow the whole thing down by roughly 12x at the default state. Target, measured on a 60 px strip at 20 fps: ~2.4 pixel ignitions per frame (~48/s, i.e. each pixel re-igniting about 0.8 times per second). The port's untouched default currently produces ~29.4 ignitions per frame, which is close to every other pixel re-rolling every single frame.

Make the fade tail visible at the default. The original's per-pixel brightness decays by a factor ~0.90 per frame at 20 fps (half-life ~0.33 s, visible tail ~1-1.5 s), which is what makes its waterfall a field of tall vertical streaks. At the port's default the decay is fast enough that no pixel keeps its color for even two frames — there is no 'fade' left in 'blink fade'.

Rescale (or drop) the Speed dial. The original has no controls, and the original's look sits at the very bottom of the port's current dial range — so the entire usable range of the port is faster than the pattern ever is. If the dial stays, re-centre it so mid-scale reproduces the original (2.4 ignitions/frame, 0.33 s fade half-life) and the ends give slower/faster around that; note also that the original's control list is empty, so a port with no dial at all would be the closer match on control surface.

After rescaling, trim ~2x off the ignition rate and ~15% off the decay speed even at the slow end: at sliderSpeed=0 the port still fires 4.90 ignitions/frame against the original's 2.41, and its half-life is ~0.28 s against ~0.33 s.

Nothing needs changing in color: hue is uniformly distributed and fully saturated on both sides, peak-brightness distribution and lit fraction already match, both sides are correctly time-based (fps-invariant), and there is no spatial motion on either side. The fix is purely the temporal rate and the dial's range.
